C: Milo wants the neighborhood mural to depict ordinary market workers in muted colors. The committee members who control future commissions prefer bright historical heroes and warn that residents may mock his idea. Should Milo defend the design he believes in or change it to secure the committee’s approval?

A: A farming cooperative fines members who deliver grain above the agreed moisture limit. Treasurer Ruth receives a damp load from an elderly farmer whose dryer failed and whose medical bills consumed his repair money; waiving the fine helps him survive but treats compliant farmers differently. Should Ruth excuse his penalty or apply the cooperative's rule without exception?
B: A scholarship requires every recipient to maintain eighty percent attendance. Administrator Joel sees that a refugee student fell just below the threshold while attending immigration appointments and will leave college without funding, yet other students lost awards under the same rule. Should Joel renew her scholarship as an exception or enforce the attendance standard equally?
C: A wholesaler wants three hundred peach crates packed by morning to catch the only train to market. Grower Helena can ship on time after quick visual sorting, or inspect every peach for bruising and miss the train, preserving quality but losing the week's buyers. Should Helena dispatch the crates quickly or delay them for careful inspection?

A: Luis keeps an emergency reserve for the bakery's aging oven, since a breakdown would stop all sales. His only delivery driver needs a deposit for accessible housing after an accident left her using a wheelchair. Giving her the money would secure the apartment but could leave the bakery unable to reopen after a failure. Should Luis help?
B: Hannah has one grant payment left to preserve frozen samples that underpin her independent laboratory's contracts. A retired technician who trained her needs a costly hearing aid to communicate with his family and cannot obtain assistance. Paying for it would help him now but might destroy years of samples. Should Hannah use the grant money?
C: A family tailor can install computer-guided cutting equipment that reduces fabric waste and allows new designs. His mother, who still works beside him, wants to preserve the hand-cut method taught through four generations, even though production will remain limited. Should he modernize the workshop or continue the inherited practice?

A: A rural clinic can begin using a new patient-record system on Monday, meeting a funding deadline but leaving staff with only basic testing. Delaying one month would allow careful migration and verification, while patients continue waiting through slow paper searches. Should the clinic launch quickly or postpone until every record and workflow has been thoroughly checked?
B: A cabinetmaker can deliver restaurant tables before opening night if he skips the final sanding and uses a fast finish. Completing them properly would create smoother, longer-lasting furniture but force the restaurant to open with rented tables. Should he meet the promised date with adequate work or delay delivery to achieve his normal standard?
C: A counselor is asked to explain her own history with grief during a hospital support group. Sharing it could encourage patients to speak freely and strengthen trust, but the story includes family details she has always guarded. Should she disclose the personal experience or maintain her privacy while guiding the discussion more distantly?

A: Jamal has followed a twelve-week swimming plan and scheduled a demanding interval session for this evening. There is no race or deadline, and he feels healthy, but friends have opened the garden fire and offered him a hammock and cold lemonade. Should he complete the training that builds endurance or spend the warm evening relaxing with them?
B: Ruth practices interpreting medical scans for an advanced certification she hopes to earn next year. After dinner, her study schedule calls for reviewing forty cases, but a deep armchair and a new mystery film promise immediate pleasure after a routine shift. Should Ruth work through the cases or settle in for the comfortable evening?
C: A professional goalkeeper is offered a starting place with a championship contender in another country. The transfer could lead to international selection, but it would separate her from the teammates and extended family she sees throughout every week. Staying means remaining a reserve with fewer honors. Should she chase the higher level or preserve her close daily ties?

A: Dr. Chen can become chief surgeon by transferring to the hospital's distant flagship campus. The promotion would bring authority, better cases, and recognition after years of training, but her spouse cannot relocate and their twin sons have just settled into school. Should she take the leadership post or remain with her family and current team?
B: Omar, a city planner, has been chosen to oversee a nationally visible rail expansion in the capital. Accepting would accelerate his career, yet his partner runs a local shop and his closest friends depend on their standing Sunday gatherings after several hard years. Should Omar move for the project or remain rooted in the city they share?
C: A clinic receptionist has saved enough to replace the failing boiler in her flat before winter. A regular patient arrives unable to pay for insulin until payday and faces several dangerous days without it. Covering the prescription would delay the repair and leave her own home unreliable. Should she protect her savings or buy the patient's medication?

A: Rosa intends to complete an online programming course by practicing after dinner for four months. Her demanding shifts make the sofa and television deeply appealing, yet missing sessions will leave her unable to build the portfolio required for better work. Should Rosa maintain the nightly coding routine or give herself the relaxing evenings she wants now?
B: A recreational swimmer plans six months of early-morning training before his first long-distance race. Cold dawns make staying under the blankets much more pleasant, and nobody depends on his participation, but frequent skipped sessions will undermine the endurance he hopes to gain. Should he follow the demanding training schedule or choose the immediate comfort of sleeping later?
C: A software company has opened every release with the founder personally ringing an old brass bell. A new automated deployment process would launch updates faster and reduce coordination, but it would eliminate the ceremony employees have shared since the first product shipped. Should the team adopt automatic releases or preserve the bell-ringing tradition?

A: A gallery promised to unveil a restored mural during Saturday’s festival. Opening then requires leaving small cracks untreated and colors matched under artificial light; three additional weeks would allow complete stabilization but miss the event that attracted donors. Should the conservator finish for Saturday or delay the unveiling to ensure durable work?
B: A hospital needs printed discharge guides for a new cardiac unit by tomorrow. Staff can adapt general material immediately without a full readability review, while careful testing with patients takes ten days and leaves nurses explaining everything verbally. Should the unit distribute the quick version or wait for instructions verified to be clear and accurate?
C: Composer Eli can join an improvising ensemble touring small venues without set programs or guaranteed audiences. His current opera company offers another fixed season with contracted pay and familiar repertoire. The experimental tour may produce remarkable work or collapse early. Should Eli explore it or remain with the secure company?

A: A restaurant owner discovers that his oldest friend, the head chef, has been relabeling yesterday’s seafood as fresh. When a health inspector asks who changed the date stickers, naming the chef could end his career and their friendship. Giving another explanation would conceal what happened. How should the owner answer the inspector?
B: Marisol learns that her cousin, a city licensing clerk, backdated a permit so a struggling shop could avoid closure. An auditor asks Marisol, who witnessed the change, whether the permit was issued on time. A truthful reply may cost her cousin his job; denying it protects him through a lie. What should Marisol say?
C: A tailor receives an order for thirty school uniforms needed for Monday’s opening ceremony. She can finish them by Sunday only by skipping reinforced seams and final fittings, while proper construction requires delivery on Wednesday. Families need clothing for the ceremony, but rushed garments may fail quickly. Should she deliver on time or take longer to make them well?

A: For forty years, a puppet theater has used hand-painted cloth backdrops changed by visible stagehands. Digital projections would allow richer settings and attract younger audiences, but retiring the cloth would end a craft passed between generations of performers. Should the director introduce projected scenery or preserve the theater's traditional handmade staging?
B: Every spring, residents paint the neighborhood underpass together using brushes and a design chosen at a public picnic. A design firm offers a durable printed mural that can be installed in one day, though it would end the annual communal ritual. Should organizers accept the modern installation or continue the shared painting tradition?
C: An orchestra treasurer has saved ticket revenue to repair the only concert piano. A young guest musician loses her violin in a house fire and cannot afford a rental for next week's audition. Helping her would postpone the piano repair and cancel rehearsals. Should the treasurer protect the orchestra's reserve or fund the violin rental?

A: Archivist Paula intends to index twenty municipal photographs each Saturday until the neglected collection becomes searchable. A sunny morning invites her to linger over coffee on the balcony, and nobody expects immediate results, yet postponing the repetitive entries will keep residents waiting months longer. Should Paula complete today's indexing target or enjoy an unstructured morning off?
B: Ramon is teaching himself programming by solving one difficult exercise before playing games each evening. Today's problem has resisted him for an hour, while his friends are already online starting a tournament; leaving it preserves a fun night but interrupts the steady effort needed to change careers. Should Ramon keep working through the exercise or join the game now?
C: The water department can reopen a repaired neighborhood pipe by noon if supervisor Beth approves the standard pressure test. She wants an additional camera inspection to catch hidden cracks, which would improve reliability but leave homes without water until evening. Should Beth restore service quickly after the basic test or delay it for the more thorough inspection?

A: A dental clinic charges a cancellation fee whenever a patient misses an appointment without one day's notice. Mrs. Bell was absent because the only bus from her village broke down and she cannot spare the fee from her pension. Should the clinic enforce the same charge she agreed to pay?
B: Registration for a charity race closes at midnight with no late entries. Aaron applies the next morning after spending the night finding shelter for his family following an apartment fire. Admitting him would show compassion, but runners delayed by other crises were previously refused. Should organizers add Aaron to the race?
C: A maternity center can replace its customary nursery, where newborns sleep together under nurses' care, with round-the-clock rooming-in beside parents. The new practice may support feeding and bonding, but generations of local families value the rest and familiar nursery rituals after birth. Should the center make the change?

A: A newly appointed librarian wants to replace formal silence rules with conversational study zones. Her family, senior staff, and longtime patrons expect her to preserve the strict atmosphere and warn that they will oppose her leadership. Should she implement the library she believes residents need or keep the old rules to retain their approval?
B: A composer wants her commissioned memorial piece to include street sounds recorded near the deceased artist's home. The orchestra and the artist's family expect a conventional string work and may reject anything else. Should she follow her own artistic judgment or write the traditional music that would secure their acceptance?
C: A transit director can receive a substantial bonus by signing a contract for cheap diesel buses before year-end. The deal improves his personal finances, but the fleet would emit more pollution across crowded neighborhoods for a decade. Should he take the rewarded contract or forgo the bonus to reduce the diffuse harm to residents?

A: Marine researcher Soraya can join an exploratory voyage to an unmapped vent field where the crew may discover unknown species, but weather and sampling success are uncertain. A funded laboratory placement offers guaranteed data, a fixed schedule, and established methods, though little room for discovery. Should Soraya take the open-ended voyage or choose the predictable laboratory project?
B: Residents give Mateo a vacant lot for a summer community project. He can let volunteers improvise gardens, play areas, and gathering spaces as ideas emerge, risking unfinished work, or follow a contractor's fixed plan for a modest park with certified equipment and a guaranteed opening date. Should Mateo support the evolving volunteer design or select the dependable standard plan?
C: At her institute's annual field survey, geologist Nia wants to replace handwritten notebooks with tablets that attach coordinates and photographs to each observation. The senior team values the marked paper volumes used for fifty years and fears losing the craft of careful field notes. Should Nia introduce digital records or continue the institute's longstanding notebook tradition?

A: A college wants its new chemistry course online before enrollment closes tomorrow. Designer Renee can publish the lectures with basic captions and quizzes, or spend another week checking terminology, adding accessible diagrams, and testing every exercise, costing the course its first cohort. Should Renee release the workable course immediately or wait until the materials are carefully finished?
B: After a storm, the council wants a pedestrian bridge reopened before Monday's commute. Engineer Idris can approve a rapid standard repair, or keep it closed another ten days while crews replace hidden corroded fittings and document each joint thoroughly. Should Idris restore access quickly or delay reopening to ensure the repair's quality?
C: Headteacher Miriam proposes replacing the school's handwritten graduation ledger with searchable digital records and printed certificates. Former pupils return each year to sign the leather-bound volume, and staff consider that act a link to generations before them. Should Miriam introduce the digital system or preserve the traditional ledger and its annual signing ritual?

A: A mining company offers geologist Lara a highly paid consulting role mapping untouched mountain deposits. The income would clear her mortgage, but successful surveys would enable roads and extraction across habitat used by many species and downstream villages. Should Lara accept the lucrative mapping contract or refuse it because of the broad environmental and community costs?
B: Procurement officer Dean can earn free personal travel by choosing an airline rewards card for all municipal bookings. Its fares are consistently higher, spreading extra costs across thousands of taxpayers, while the points would fund a holiday he otherwise cannot afford. Should Dean select the card for his private reward or use the cheaper option for the public budget?
C: Botanist Rina can explore an isolated valley where undocumented plants may yield an unexpected discovery, though access and results are uncertain. A greenhouse project offers confirmed specimens, controlled conditions, and a guaranteed publication schedule but little surprise. Should Rina pursue the unpredictable field expedition or choose the secure research project with reliable outcomes?

A: A college promises applicants admission decisions this Friday. Releasing them then requires relying on automated transcript summaries that staff know occasionally miss unusual qualifications. Manual review would take another fortnight and leave families waiting, but every application would receive careful judgment. Should the college announce decisions quickly or delay them for reliable review?
B: A furniture maker can deliver twelve café tables before opening day if apprentices assemble them without time for final leveling and finish tests. Delaying one week forces the café to rent temporary tables but lets the maker correct every wobble and seal each surface properly. Should she meet the opening date or complete the order carefully?
C: An adult-education center removes students after three missed classes, a rule that created places for people on the waiting list last month. Hawa reaches three while arranging temporary housing after a flood. Should the coordinator let her remain because of the disaster or enforce the attendance rule consistently?

A: During peer review, a chemist recognizes data copied from an unpublished draft written by his former mentor. Reporting the evidence would correct the paper and may start a misconduct case against the person who secured his first position. Should the chemist document the copied results or protect his mentor from professional harm?
B: A gallery assistant learns that her closest friend submitted a copied illustration to a juried exhibition and claimed it as original. Correcting the record would protect the genuine artist but could disqualify her friend and fracture years of trust. Should the assistant tell the curator the truth or stay silent to shield her friend?
C: A laboratory charges every visiting researcher the same fee for damaged glassware. One student breaks a flask while rushing home to care for his father and asks to have the charge waived because his stipend is nearly gone. Other students have paid after accidents. Should the manager enforce the standard fee or make an exception for his hardship?

A: Eleanor wants her graduation exhibition to feature rough charcoal portraits of night-shift workers. Her tutors and classmates urge her to show the polished landscapes that previously won prizes, and they may judge the portraits as an embarrassing departure. Should she present the work she prefers or select the paintings most likely to earn their approval?
B: Theo wants to convert his inherited field into a wildflower meadow and keep only a small flock of sheep. His farming relatives expect him to continue their high-yield wheat operation and warn that neighbors will consider his choice unserious. Should Theo follow his preferred way of farming or maintain the practice that wins their respect?
C: A film studio offers Amara a large location fee to shoot a commercial in protected dunes near her home. Truck access would damage vegetation and increase erosion along a coast used by thousands of residents, though she would receive the payment directly. Should Amara accept the profitable production or refuse because of the broader harm?

A: While preparing quarterly accounts, florist Dana discovers that her brother and co-owner has been deleting cash sales from the tax records. Correcting the return would expose his actions, bring penalties, and possibly break their partnership, but signing the current figures makes her endorse a lie. Should Dana report the true sales or protect her brother and their shop?
B: Jon reviews receipts for a neighborhood food pantry and sees that his closest friend claimed reimbursement for supplies she never purchased. Revealing the false claim would preserve an honest grant report but could remove her from the committee and end their friendship during a difficult divorce. Should Jon correct the accounts publicly or remain loyal to his friend?
C: A beverage distributor offers cafe owner Suki a profitable contract if she switches from washable glasses to individually wrapped plastic cups. The savings would fund a second location and raise her income, while thousands of discarded cups would add waste collected and processed by the whole city. Should Suki accept the contract for expansion or keep reusable service to reduce the wider burden?

A: Maya has been offered the lead role on an Antarctic climate study, a rare chance to direct her own research and strengthen her bid for tenure. The eighteen-month posting would make her miss her sister's wedding and leave her aging father without their weekly visits. Should Maya accept the expedition appointment?
B: After years in a neighborhood orchestra, Daniel is invited to tour Europe as the featured cellist, with press coverage that could launch a solo career. Rehearsals and travel would keep him away during his partner's first year with their adopted child and end the Sunday dinners his parents depend on. Should Daniel join the tour?
C: A marine biologist can spend her grant on an untested deep-sea survey near volcanic vents, where a new species may be found but storms could ruin the entire season's work. The alternative is a mapped coastal site with modest, dependable data and an established rescue plan. Which research voyage should she fund?

A: An orchard must ship young trees before a seasonal freight discount expires Friday. Packing them that quickly means skipping individual root inspections, while holding the shipment for five days allows damaged stock to be removed but raises costs and delays customers’ planting. Should the nursery ship promptly or wait until every tree is carefully checked?
B: Volunteers can reopen a storm-damaged community hall before Saturday’s wedding by patching the roof and painting over damp marks. A thorough repair requires replacing hidden timbers and postponing events for a month. Should the committee provide the hall quickly with temporary work or delay reopening until the building is properly restored?
C: A young farmer can direct a major greenhouse enterprise abroad, gaining the experience needed to run large agricultural companies. Accepting means leaving the siblings who work beside him and the village gatherings that anchor his week. Should he pursue the prominent position or stay within the family and community he values?

A: A mobile-phone company offers Sara a personal fee to place a large illuminated billboard on the community center she manages. The sign would shine into hundreds of nearby homes and increase neighborhood electricity use, but her contract allows her to keep the payment. Should Sara accept the income or protect residents from the shared disturbance?
B: A textbook publisher offers a principal a private speaking fee if his school replaces reusable books annually with new workbooks. The arrangement would increase paper consumption and disposal across every class while benefiting him personally. Should he recommend the yearly replacement or reject the offer because of the collective environmental cost?
C: For forty years, residents have opened their summer festival by carrying handmade lanterns along the canal. Organizers propose replacing the procession with a drone light display that offers new patterns but ends the craft nights and familiar walk. Should the neighborhood adopt the digital spectacle or preserve its established celebration?

A: A bookstore owner is seeking support from neighboring merchants after missing several shared events. Explaining that she is separating from her spouse could restore trust and help them coordinate around her availability, yet it would make an intimate family change public. Should she disclose the separation or protect her privacy despite continued doubts about her commitment?
B: A development team is frustrated by Ravi's refusal to join video calls. Revealing that a facial condition makes cameras distressing could help colleagues collaborate with him and stop speculation, but he has kept the diagnosis private throughout his career. Should Ravi explain the condition openly or retain his privacy and accept the team's misunderstanding?
C: A shop manager learns that her sister, who handles accounts, changed the sales totals presented to their lender. Correcting the figures would prevent a false loan decision but could lead to fraud charges against someone she loves. Should the manager give the bank accurate records or protect her sister from the likely consequences?

A: Biologist Evan has saved a small emergency fund while working on short contracts. His former lab technician calls because her elderly cat needs surgery by Friday and she cannot cover the final eight hundred dollars; lending it may save the cat but leave Evan unable to pay rent if his contract ends. Should Evan provide the surgery money or preserve his emergency savings?
B: Adjunct lecturer Farah has enough set aside to replace her unreliable car before winter. A student she mentors has been accepted to a teaching conference but cannot afford the registration and train fare, and missing it could close an early career opportunity. Should Farah fund the student's trip or keep the money for dependable transportation?
C: During a joint experiment, Leah discovers that her longtime colleague Marcus entered several measurements incorrectly, making their celebrated result unsupported. Reporting the error before publication protects the scientific record but could cost Marcus his fellowship and damage a friendship built over twelve years. Should Leah disclose the faulty measurements to the journal or protect Marcus from the consequences?

A: Teacher Malcolm promised his graduating class a final weekend review before their licensing exam. On Saturday morning he wakes with laryngitis and a fever; the substitute does not know the material, yet speaking for four hours could prolong his illness. Should Malcolm conduct the review his students rely on or cancel it and recover?
B: Janelle coordinates volunteers rebuilding a wheelchair ramp for an elderly neighbor, and the concrete delivery cannot be moved. A strained back makes lifting painful, while several first-time volunteers need her hands-on direction to finish before rain arrives. Should Janelle work through the pain to meet her commitment or stay home and let her back heal?
C: Professor Wei is invited to deliver a short keynote overseas, an appearance likely to raise his profile and consulting income. The trip requires two long flights for a twenty-minute talk, despite an equally useful video option, adding emissions that contribute to a burden shared far beyond the conference. Should Wei fly for the career benefit or present remotely to limit that impact?

A: A streaming developer can earn a large performance bonus by enabling ultra-high-resolution playback automatically for every user. The change increases engagement and her compensation, but multiplies electricity use in data centers and devices worldwide. Should she activate the profitable default or accept a smaller bonus to limit the environmental burden across millions of viewers?
B: A private clinic owner can raise profits by switching every disposable tray to a cheaper mixed-plastic version. The trays meet regulations, but cannot be recycled and would add tonnes of waste to regional landfills each year. Should she take the substantial savings or pay more to reduce the clinic's diffuse environmental impact?
C: A programmer is offered a senior role at an overseas company whose product she has admired for years. The move could establish her international career, but would end daily life with her partner and remove her from the close group of friends who share childcare. Should she accept the position or remain with her established circle?

A: A wrestling tournament disqualifies anyone above the division limit at weigh-in. Keiko is slightly over because medication for a serious allergic reaction caused sudden water retention. Letting her compete would recognize an unusual medical hardship but bend the cutoff enforced against every other athlete. Should officials admit Keiko?
B: A conservatory withdraws scholarships after four unexcused rehearsals. Malik missed his fourth while attending his sister's funeral abroad and cannot afford tuition without the award. Making an exception would acknowledge his loss, while other students who exceeded the limit already lost funding. Should the conservatory restore Malik's scholarship?
C: During a decisive football match, an assistant referee sees his childhood friend deliberately handle the ball before scoring, though the main referee misses it. Reporting the offense will erase the goal and may end their friendship; staying silent would let an untrue result stand. Should the assistant signal the violation?

A: Every morning before her clinic shift, Dr. Shah studies Spanish so she can eventually speak directly with more patients. Today she would prefer another hour under the blankets, with no urgent appointment or examination forcing her up. Skipping makes the morning easier but interrupts the routine producing gradual improvement. Should she rise to study or keep sleeping?
B: Colin spends three quiet evenings each week learning bookkeeping so he can manage his repair shop without outside help. Tonight, the accounts workbook is waiting, but the pub downstairs has live music and a comfortable booth reserved by friends. No bill is due tomorrow. Should Colin follow his learning routine or join the easy night out?
C: Leah prefers to train as a hospice nurse, drawn to long conversations with patients nearing death. Her parents and nursing classmates expect her to enter intensive care, which they consider more impressive and have celebrated publicly. Choosing hospice may disappoint them and reduce their praise. Which specialty should Leah select?

A: Elena is offered a promotion to direct emergency medicine at a renowned city hospital, giving her authority to reshape the department and advance her career. The move would take her family away from grandparents who provide daily childcare and from neighbors who supported them through her son's illness. Should Elena accept the directorship?
B: A cooperative has invited Marcus to manage its largest vineyard, a position that could establish him as a leading winemaker. He would have to relocate before harvest, leaving the small farming community where his cousins share equipment and where he has spent every evening caring for the family orchard. Should Marcus take the vineyard job?
C: A clinic owner can replace reusable examination gowns with cheaper disposable ones, increasing her annual income enough to renovate her office. The change would send thousands of plastic-lined garments to landfill each year and add emissions from weekly deliveries, while reusable gowns keep laundry and replacement costs high. Should she switch to disposables?

A: Theo wants to master portrait drawing before applying to art school next year. Doing fifty careful sketches each week would steadily improve his technique, but spending evenings at the neighborhood cafe is easier and more enjoyable after work. Should Theo keep the demanding practice target for his future skill or relax with friends whenever he feels tired?
B: An adult learner has committed to studying Spanish vocabulary during every morning commute so she can read novels without translation next summer. Casual games on her phone offer effortless entertainment now, while the repeated drills feel tedious. Should she persist with the daily lessons for later fluency or spend the journey on easier pleasures?
C: A muralist can finish a school corridor before parents' night by painting directly over several uneven repairs. Taking four extra days to prepare the wall would produce clean lines and lasting color, but visitors would see an unfinished space at the event. Should she deliver the mural by Thursday or delay it to ensure durable workmanship?

A: Carla has saved enough from weekend work to repair the roof of her own aging house before the rainy season. Another volunteer at the neighborhood pantry needs a deposit for accessible housing after an accident. Paying it would secure his move, but Carla’s home could suffer expensive water damage. Should she fund the deposit or protect her house?
B: A swim instructor has one month of expenses saved after the pool announced possible closures. One of his adult students needs a prosthetic adjustment to continue walking without pain, and her appointment will be canceled unless she pays tomorrow. Covering it would erase his unemployment buffer. Should he keep his savings or pay for her care?
C: Volunteers promised to reopen the neighborhood playground by Friday, when school holidays begin. The new wooden ramp can be installed by then, but sealing and testing it properly requires four more days; delaying disappoints families who planned to use it immediately. Should the coordinator open on schedule or wait until the workmanship is fully reliable?

A: A family restaurant has served one fixed Sunday menu from the grandmother's handwritten recipes for sixty years. Introducing rotating regional dishes could draw new customers, but regulars and relatives consider the unchanged meal part of the family's continuity. Should the new owner redesign the menu or preserve the traditional Sunday service?
B: A primary school has taught local history through an annual walking tour led by retired residents. Interactive classroom archives would offer more sources and work in bad weather, yet the walk preserves a valued exchange between children and elders. Should teachers replace it with the digital course or keep the long-standing community tour?
C: A hardware shop owner has reserved cash to replace a delivery van that may fail soon. His longtime cashier needs an emergency deposit to escape an unsafe flat with her daughter. Lending the money could leave the shop unable to make deliveries. Should the owner protect the vehicle fund or help his employee move immediately?

A: Stage manager Ruth promised to call every cue for her community theater's opening night, and no understudy knows the complicated lighting sequence. Hours before curtain she experiences chest pain and is advised to seek immediate evaluation; canceling disappoints a sold-out audience, while continuing could endanger her health. Should Ruth go to the hospital or fulfill her opening-night responsibility?
B: Cafe owner Ben has bronchitis and his doctor prescribed two days of complete rest. His only employee calls out just before a prepaid memorial reception, leaving the grieving family without the meal Ben agreed to provide. Should Ben open the kitchen and honor the booking or close the cafe to protect his recovery?
C: A gallery charges every exhibitor the same late fee when work arrives after the installation deadline. Curator Mina's former teacher misses it because she has been caring for her terminally ill husband and cannot afford the charge, though others have paid after difficult weeks. Should Mina waive the fee for her teacher or enforce the rule equally?

A: Dev has set aside his freelance income for three months of rent after losing a major software client. His former intern calls because her laptop died before a paid coding assessment, and she cannot afford another. Lending her his backup machine risks delaying his own work and income. Should Dev keep the equipment available or help her take the assessment?
B: A substitute teacher has saved a small emergency fund after months of irregular shifts. One pupil's father asks her to cover the fee for a required exam because an unexpected eviction consumed the family's cash. Paying would let the student graduate, but leave the teacher unable to handle her own next missed paycheck. Should she retain the fund or pay his fee?
C: A startup can let volunteers install experimental plug-ins in its coding platform, encouraging unexpected tools and discoveries. Security staff warn that an unreviewed plug-in could corrupt users' projects, while mandatory approval would make every extension predictable but restrict experimentation. Should the team open the platform to independent plug-ins or require a protected, reviewed catalog?

A: A hotel requests sixty dining chairs from carpenter Omar before its opening next week. He can meet the date with a simple finish and standard joints, or spend ten additional days strengthening each frame and matching the stain precisely, forcing the hotel to rent furniture. Should Omar deliver acceptable chairs quickly or delay them for finer workmanship?
B: A laboratory needs preliminary soil results before officials decide where to drill emergency wells. Analyst Yuki can send automated readings this afternoon, or spend three days rerunning outliers and manually checking contamination controls, delaying the decision. Should Yuki provide the early usable results or wait until the analysis is thoroughly verified?
C: Bakery owner Felix discovers that his best friend and business partner substituted cheap margarine while advertising their pastries as all-butter. Correcting the labels and informing customers protects the truth but could destroy his friend's reputation and their partnership. Should Felix disclose the substitution or remain silent to protect the person who built the bakery with him?

A: A cycling captain’s teammates interpret his repeated solo training as arrogance. He is actually caring for a partner undergoing fertility treatment and must arrange rides around appointments. Telling the team could repair cooperation and explain his schedule, but it exposes private medical details belonging to their household. Should he disclose the reason or remain silent?
B: Nina’s classmates are frustrated when she declines evening study sessions. She has recently become the sole carer for a parent with dementia, and explaining this could rebuild trust and help the group schedule daytime meetings. It would also reveal a family condition she promised to keep private. Should Nina tell them or protect the family’s confidentiality?
C: A tennis coach discovers that her lifelong friend entered a junior player under a false age to qualify for a tournament. Officials ask whether the birth date on the registration is accurate. Correcting it would disqualify the child and expose her friend to sanctions; confirming it would be dishonest. What should the coach say?

A: Nora has been offered a solo exhibition at a prestigious Berlin gallery during the month her local printmaking collective is preparing its tenth anniversary show. Berlin could transform her career, but accepting would leave the five artists who built the collective with her to mount their milestone event alone. Should Nora pursue the solo exhibition or stay with her longtime collaborators?
B: A professional cycling team wants Darius to attend its distant development camp immediately, giving him his first credible route into elite racing. His neighborhood club, where his closest friends train together, is entering a regional relay that same month and has no replacement rider. Should Darius leave for the development camp or race beside his club?
C: Elena bought a demanding piano method course to prepare for an audition six months away. Tonight's scheduled practice covers scales she dislikes, while her favorite film has just appeared online and her friends are gathering to watch it with takeout. Skipping one evening would feel pleasant but weaken the routine she needs to improve. Should Elena practice or join the film night?

A: Lena has kept the final month's reserve needed to cover rent at her struggling cafe. Her dishwasher reveals that his child needs a specialist appointment requiring immediate payment, which he cannot raise. Giving him an advance may prevent the appointment from being canceled but could leave the cafe unable to open. Should Lena preserve the reserve or advance his wages?
B: A theater costume designer has saved enough to replace the sewing machine that repeatedly stalls before deadlines. Her longtime stagehand needs money for a train ticket to reach his hospitalized sister tonight. Buying the ticket could reunite them, but another machine failure may cost the designer her next contract. Should she keep the replacement fund or pay his fare?
C: A bookstore charges every stallholder the same nonrefundable fee for its annual makers' fair. One ceramic artist misses the cancellation deadline because she was caring for her injured son and asks for her money back. Refunding her would ease a real hardship but break the rule applied to three others. Should the owner enforce the fee or grant her an exception?

A: For next season's opera, the director can replace painted scenery with projected landscapes that shift during each aria. The technology would enable new visual effects, but the theater's painters and longtime audience cherish the handmade sets that have defined performances for decades. Should the director commission the projections?
B: A family grocery can install self-checkout stations and electronic shelf labels, freeing staff to prepare online orders. Regular customers value chatting with the cashiers and watching prices written on cards each morning, a routine the owner's parents maintained for forty years. Should the grocery adopt the new system?
C: A muralist is offered a prominent yearlong residency in Berlin that could bring international commissions and her first museum exhibition. Accepting would pull her away from the neighborhood art collective she helped found and make her miss weekly dinners with her siblings. Should she leave for the residency?

A: Irene wants her next physics study to replicate a famous result that she doubts, even though her laboratory director and peers consider replication dull and expect her to pursue a fashionable quantum device. Following their choice would earn enthusiastic support; following her judgment may isolate the project. Which study should Irene undertake?
B: After inheriting a grain farm, Pavel wants to convert one pasture to alpacas and learn textile production. His parents and neighboring farmers expect him to continue the respected wheat operation and say they will take his decision seriously only if he does. Should Pavel follow his own plan?
C: A laboratory has developed a low-cost water contamination test before flood season. Shipping it this week would give relief teams early results, but engineers have not completed calibration across extreme temperatures; six more weeks would produce a more reliable kit after the immediate demand peaks. When should the laboratory release it?

A: Team captain Zoe recently began treatment for an eating disorder. Explaining it to teammates could help them avoid harmful comments and understand why she sometimes trains separately, but the diagnosis is intimate and she fears it spreading through the league. Should Zoe speak openly with the team or keep her health information confidential?
B: Physician Elena is returning to work after caring for a partner with addiction. Sharing that experience at a staff meeting could help colleagues understand her interest in compassionate treatment and invite honest discussion, but it would expose her partner's private struggle as well as her own. Should Elena tell the department or keep the family experience private?
C: Boxer Marcus plans daily footwork drills for three months to correct a weakness before his next bout. Tonight his favorite restaurant is hosting a long tasting dinner, and the drills feel tedious after work, but skipping them weakens the consistency improvement requires. Should Marcus complete his training session or spend the evening enjoying the meal?

A: A city planner can pilot an on-demand night bus whose routes would change with passenger requests, though demand and operating costs remain unknown. The approved alternative adds one fixed evening service with guaranteed ridership from prior surveys. Should she test the flexible experiment or implement the predictable route residents already understand?
B: A newly qualified nurse can join a relief team that assigns members to different clinics each week, offering broad experience but uncertain hours and conditions. A rehabilitation center nearby guarantees a protected schedule, training plan, and permanent contract. Should he enter the changing relief work or select the stable clinical post?
C: The housing office cancels applications when tenants miss two verification appointments, a rule already applied to several residents. Mrs. Evans missed her second because her wheelchair-accessible taxi never arrived, and eviction proceedings begin next week. Should the caseworker reopen her application as an exception or enforce the same deadline used for everyone?

A: Reviewing a patient's chart, Dr. Chen notices that his friend and colleague entered the wrong medication dose, then quietly corrected the prescription without documenting the error. Recording what happened may expose his friend to discipline, while silence leaves the patient's medical history inaccurate. Should Dr. Chen file the correction and incident report?
B: A lecturer learns that her former roommate, now teaching beside her, gave one class advance access to questions used in a university examination. Telling the faculty board would threaten her friend's position; saying nothing would allow an untrue account of equal testing to stand. Should the lecturer report what she learned?
C: A patient with kidney failure can learn home dialysis, choosing treatment times herself and traveling between sessions, but equipment problems would have to be handled without staff nearby. Continuing at the clinic provides constant supervision and a fixed routine, though it restricts work and family plans. Which arrangement should she choose?

A: The residents maintaining a shared orchard agreed to prune two rows each weekend so the trees will produce well next year. Paul’s assigned morning is cool and clear, but he wants to eat breakfast slowly and lounge beside the radio. Nobody will suffer today if he skips. Should Paul do the planned work or take an easy morning?
B: Mara has practiced the cello for ninety minutes daily to prepare a difficult suite she hopes to master by winter. This evening, she feels fine but wants a long bath and casual television instead of repeating awkward passages. There is no rehearsal tomorrow. Should she maintain the demanding practice or choose immediate comfort?
C: Dev volunteered to coordinate a river cleanup and is the only person with keys to the equipment shed. He wakes with a fever and aching muscles on the morning seventy volunteers are due to arrive. Canceling wastes their preparation, while attending may slow his recovery. Should Dev rest at home or fulfill the role he accepted?

A: A middle school can let students spend one term designing independent projects without preset subjects or outcomes. Some may discover interests teachers never anticipated, but others could finish with little assessable work; the standard curriculum guarantees covered material. Should the principal authorize open projects or keep every class on the established, predictable course?
B: A research vessel reaches an unmapped cove where unusual algae may be growing. The captain can enter and let scientists collect rare samples, but navigation charts show uncertain depths; remaining offshore ensures the crew returns safely with existing data. Should the expedition explore the cove or follow the surveyed route home?
C: A lecturer is shortlisted for a prestigious post that requires moving overseas and teaching through most holidays. Winning it would accelerate her academic career, but she would leave the siblings and friends with whom she shares weekly meals and mutual care. Should she pursue the appointment or remain near the people who shape her daily life?

A: Marcus has budgeted his remaining scholarship money for textbooks and meals through the semester. His classmate, who has been sleeping in a car, asks for help with a hostel deposit after the campus shelter fills. Paying could give her a safe week indoors but force Marcus to skip required books. Should he keep the money for school or cover her room?
B: The owner of a repair shop has enough cash either to replace a failing compressor or to help his only mechanic after her apartment burns. Without the machine, the shop may lose jobs and threaten his livelihood; without a deposit, she and her son remain in a motel. Should he secure the equipment or use the money to house his employee?
C: A private tutoring company can double its margin by replacing reusable workbooks with cheap single-use packets mailed to every student each week. The switch would raise the owner's income, but thousands of coated pages and plastic sleeves would be discarded monthly. Should she adopt the profitable packets or accept lower earnings to reduce the waste imposed on others?

A: Ravi has qualified for a national young farmers competition whose winner receives enough investment to expand a greenhouse business. The final occurs during the cooperative's annual planting weekend, when his closest neighbors share equipment and count on his seed drill. Should Ravi travel to compete for expansion funding or plant beside the cooperative that has supported him?
B: Promotion to district fire captain would give Tessa greater responsibility and the career she has worked toward, but the post uses rotating stations across the county. She would lose daily shifts with the crew whose members helped raise her children and gather at her home every Friday. Should Tessa accept the captaincy or remain with her current station crew?
C: After twisting his knee, orchard manager Owen was told to avoid slopes for a week. A sudden frost is forecast tonight, and two inexperienced workers need him to guide the placement of heaters among the hillside trees; without him, much of the crop may be lost. Should Owen work the orchard despite the risk of worsening his injury or follow his recovery instructions?

A: A publisher wants illustrator Celia's children's book delivered tomorrow for an important catalog deadline. She can submit the complete rough drawings tonight, or spend four more days correcting inconsistent characters and painting richer backgrounds, causing the title to miss the catalog. Should Celia deliver the adequate illustrations quickly or delay them until the artwork meets her standards?
B: A restaurant offers grower Malik a premium price for two hundred herb boxes by Friday. He can pack quickly after checking only the top leaves, or inspect every bunch for pests and freshness, missing the delivery window but protecting consistent quality. Should Malik send the boxes on schedule or take longer to examine and repack them carefully?
C: Gallery owner Petra learns that her closest artist friend submitted a forged residency certificate to qualify for a regional exhibition. Revealing it preserves an honest selection and correct public record but may end her friend's career after years of mutual support. Should Petra tell the selection panel the certificate is false or protect her friend by remaining silent?

A: Nina wants to make an old volunteer scheduling app reliable before the local shelter adopts it next spring. Doing so requires testing and refactoring one module every morning for four months, replacing the extra hour she normally spends in bed. Should Nina keep the daily development routine?
B: A jazz pianist could prepare a difficult solo album by practicing scales and passages for ninety minutes every evening until autumn. The routine would improve his control, but it would also replace the comfortable hours he spends lingering over dinner and listening to records. Should he follow the practice plan?
C: A product designer prefers a spare keyboard-driven interface for the budgeting tool she is building. Her investors and fellow designers expect colorful dashboards and warn that they may withdraw their endorsement if she ignores current tastes. Should she keep her own restrained design or adopt the style they approve?

A: Caleb hopes to qualify for an engineering program and has scheduled algebra exercises every Saturday until the entrance test. His friends invite him on leisurely day trips that offer immediate fun, while the worksheets promise only gradual improvement months later. Should Caleb protect his study routine or trade those difficult mornings for relaxing outings?
B: A trainee firefighter wants to pass the promotion examination in autumn. Reviewing building codes after each shift is dull compared with joining colleagues for dinner, but consistent study would prepare her for responsibilities she wants later. Should she complete the planned nightly reading or enjoy the easy social hours available now?
C: A college can let students wander an extensive cave system during a geology excursion, choosing passages that interest them. The alternative keeps everyone behind a guide on a mapped loop, where discoveries are limited but rockfalls and wrong turns are controlled. Should the instructor allow open exploration or require the predictable protected route?

A: A small software firm has tracked every bug on index cards pinned around the office since its first release. A shared digital board would support remote staff and faster searching, but founders see the handwritten wall as part of how the team remembers its history. Should the firm adopt digital tracking or preserve the card-based tradition?
B: A mountain village has dried pears on communal wooden racks for more than a century. Enclosed solar dryers would reduce spoilage and labor, yet families value gathering at the old racks and teaching children the inherited method. Should the growers install the new dryers or continue the traditional communal process?
C: A software training program requires every participant who misses a lab to pay the same rebooking fee. One apprentice was absent because her child needed emergency surgery and asks to reschedule for free. Waiving it would ease her hardship but depart from the rule enforced for others. Should the director apply the fee or grant her an exception?

A: Jonah’s university will fund his doctorate if he transfers to a campus across the country, where a leading scholar has agreed to supervise him. Leaving would interrupt the weekly care he shares for his grandfather and separate him from cousins who rely on those evenings together. Should Jonah accept the academic opportunity or remain embedded in his family’s life?
B: A rural physician has been selected for a competitive surgical fellowship in the capital, opening a path to the specialty she has always wanted. The two-year move would take her from the clinic team and neighbors who supported her through a difficult divorce. Does she leave to advance or stay with the community where she belongs?
C: During a group project, Marcus notices that panic attacks are making presentations difficult. Telling his classmates could let them divide speaking duties honestly and understand his sudden absences, but it would expose a diagnosis he has kept private from everyone at school. Should Marcus disclose his condition to the group or keep it confidential?

A: Nadia founded a neighborhood garden that now occupies most evenings with friends and relatives. A national nonprofit offers her a paid fellowship to replicate it across twenty cities, but the travel would make her largely absent from the original garden and its tight volunteer circle. Should Nadia scale her work nationally or remain present with the group that built it?
B: A marine biologist receives funding to run her own laboratory on an island research station. The appointment could establish her as a leading coral expert, but it means leaving her partner and the colleagues who have shared her fieldwork for six years. Should she depart for an independent scientific career or keep her place within her existing relationships?
C: To win residents' trust for a youth shelter, Malik considers telling the planning committee that he lived in temporary housing as a teenager. The disclosure could explain his commitment and unlock cooperation, but the experience is private and several neighbors know his family. Should Malik share that history publicly or keep it confidential despite the project's stalled support?

A: Ben has saved a month's rent for the teaching certificate exam he must retake to keep his classroom position. A student he mentors faces eviction with her mother unless they find the same amount by Friday. Paying their arrears could keep them housed but put Ben's job and apartment at risk. Should Ben give them his savings?
B: A bus dispatcher has enough personal leave to protect her wages during the quiet winter period. Her colleague's child needs daily hospital visits, and the colleague has exhausted his leave; donating her days would let him stay at the bedside but leave her without coverage if she becomes ill. Should she transfer the leave?
C: A school district can distribute newly purchased tablets next Monday, allowing students without computers to join online lessons immediately. Its technicians have tested only half the devices, and waiting two more weeks would allow full security checks and accessibility setup while students continue missing assignments. Should the district issue the tablets now?

A: A drug company offers physician Nina a generous speaking fee to recommend its branded inhaler at professional meetings. A cheaper generic works equally well, and widespread adoption of the brand would raise costs across patients and insurance pools. Should Nina accept the paid speaking role for personal income or decline to avoid imposing broader healthcare costs?
B: A manufacturer promises researcher Caleb a large patent share if he develops a single-use sensor for laboratories. The disposable model could make him wealthy, but thousands of labs would discard batteries and plastic housings after every test when a reusable design is possible. Should Caleb pursue the profitable disposable sensor or develop the lower-waste alternative?
C: Cardiologist Amara is offered leadership of a renowned urban research center, giving her a path to international recognition. Taking it means leaving the rural clinic where nurses, patients, and neighbors have become her daily circle over eight years. Should Amara accept the prestigious post or remain with the close healthcare community that depends on her presence?

A: Sam wants the community workshop to welcome unscheduled drop-ins rather than require formal memberships. His fellow organizers and closest friends say they will endorse him as coordinator only if he keeps the controlled club structure. Should Sam build the inclusive project he prefers or retain the system that earns his peers' approval?
B: A talented runner prefers trail races, while her parents and training partners expect her to compete on the track where they believe she can win medals. Moving to trails feels personally right but may disappoint the people funding and supporting her. Should she choose her favored sport or remain on the track to meet their expectations?
C: The coordinator of a housing renovation project develops vertigo before the weekend when volunteers must install windows in six occupied flats. Rest would protect her recovery, but she alone has the measurements and residents have already cleared their rooms. Should she stay home as advised or fulfill her commitment and direct the installations?

A: Farm inspector Alice finds that her cousin has been labeling ordinary eggs as free-range after storm damage confined the hens indoors. Recording the violation protects accurate sales information but could cancel the contract keeping his farm afloat, while overlooking it shields a relative through a difficult season. Should Alice file the truthful report or protect her cousin's livelihood?
B: Nurse Theo learns that his closest coworker changed a patient's fall time in the chart to make it appear that staffing rules were followed. Correcting the entry preserves an honest medical record but could lead to her suspension and leave her family without wages. Should Theo report the altered time or remain loyal to his coworker?
C: Young farmer Mira wants to replace part of the family wheat field with the herbs she enjoys growing and has already found local buyers. Her parents and neighboring farmers expect her to continue the crop that defines the family farm and dismiss herbs as unserious. Should Mira plant according to her own preference or keep wheat to retain their approval?

A: Mina joined the city planning department but wants to work in its small cycling unit because she prefers designing street-level routes. Her family expects her to pursue the prestigious diplomatic service examination, and their approval depends on seeing her enter a nationally recognized career. Which path should Mina follow?
B: A chemist wants to leave daily laboratory work for a public field station, explaining water results directly to rural communities. His research colleagues say serious scientists remain at the bench and may stop recommending him for collaborations. Should he choose the field role he prefers?
C: After a river bridge is damaged, the council can reopen one lane in ten days using temporary supports, restoring bus service quickly. A full structural repair would keep it closed for seven weeks but withstand heavy traffic and winter floods with greater reliability. Which repair plan should the council approve?

A: Neighbors have maintained their memorial garden through monthly hand-weeding days since the estate was built. A grant would install automated irrigation and low-maintenance planting, reducing labor but ending the gatherings where older residents teach children how each bed began. Should the committee redesign the garden or preserve its established communal care?
B: A rehabilitation ward has begun each morning with patients and nurses walking one slow lap together, a custom former patients still remember. Managers propose individualized app-guided sessions that adjust exercises precisely but remove the shared round. Should the ward introduce personal digital programs or retain the collective routine that defines its history?
C: A residents’ group can spend its grant on an experimental floating garden designed by local teenagers, though permits, maintenance, and survival rates remain uncertain. A contractor offers a standard paved plaza with warranties and fixed costs. Should the group attempt the evolving garden or choose the predictable protected project?

A: A nonprofit needs its donation app ready before a televised fundraiser on Sunday. Programmer Joel can launch the core payment flow after a brief test, capturing that audience, or postpone release to examine accessibility, refunds, and unusual card failures carefully. Should Joel ship the usable app before the fundraiser or delay it until the full experience is reliable?
B: A stadium's running track must reopen for school championships next week. Contractor Laila can apply one quick surface coat and meet the date, or add two carefully cured layers that provide better grip and durability but force organizers to reschedule. Should Laila finish the track quickly for the championships or delay reopening for higher-quality work?
C: A video platform offers developer Marco a large bonus to add automatic high-resolution playback as the default. The feature would increase subscriptions and his payout, but it would consume more electricity and network capacity for millions of viewers who never requested it. Should Marco pursue the bonus by enabling the feature or keep efficient playback to reduce the shared resource cost?

A: Sofia has set aside her final three hundred dollars to insure the camera she uses for paid wedding photography. Her neighbor's violin was damaged in a basement flood, and without money for repairs he will lose a confirmed orchestra audition. Helping him would leave Sofia's livelihood exposed to theft. Should Sofia pay for the repair?
B: Caleb keeps a reserve fund for veterinary bills and winter feed on his small goat farm. A nearby farmer has broken her leg and needs immediate money to hire someone to milk her herd before the animals become sick. Covering that cost would leave Caleb unprepared for trouble on his own farm. Should he help her?
C: The director of a century-old theater can replace its annual live pantomime with an interactive digital production that lets remote audiences influence the ending. The experiment may attract younger viewers, but local families and retired performers treasure the familiar songs, costumes, and shared holiday ritual. Should the theater adopt the new format?

A: A film producer will receive a substantial completion bonus if she flies actors between five cities by private jet and finishes before awards season. Commercial flights would reduce emissions greatly but miss the release date and her payment. Should she authorize the private flights?
B: A highway maintenance contractor can increase his margin by using the cheapest deicing salt on a large winter contract. Runoff from the salt will damage roadside trees and enter streams along hundreds of kilometers, while a less harmful mixture reduces his profit. Which material should he purchase?
C: A museum curator discovers documents showing that a painting donated by her closest friend has a fabricated ownership history. Publishing the true provenance would embarrass him and could expose him to legal claims; keeping the label unchanged would mislead visitors and researchers. Should she correct the museum record?

A: A software founder is negotiating with employees who distrust her sudden absences. Explaining that she is undergoing fertility treatment could restore confidence and help them plan schedules together, but it would expose intimate information she intended to keep private. Should she disclose the reason for her absences or preserve her privacy despite the team's uncertainty?
B: A playwright is asked to tell actors that the central character draws directly from his estranged brother's addiction. Revealing this could help the cast understand difficult scenes and collaborate more honestly, but it would expose a painful family history. Should he share the personal source with the company or keep it confidential?
C: An app developer can substantially increase advertising revenue by recording users' locations every few minutes. The data would enrich her personally, but the extra tracking consumes energy across millions of phones and encourages more server use and electronic turnover. Should she adopt the profitable tracking system or accept less income to reduce its widespread costs?

A: A vegetable grower can devote her largest field to rare local tomato seeds whose flavors may command high prices, though their yield and disease resistance are unknown. Planting the commercial hybrid would bring predictable harvests and established insurance coverage but reveal nothing new about the old variety. Which seed should she plant?
B: Two climbers reach a fork below the summit. An unmapped ridge might offer an extraordinary ascent and a clear view, but its snow conditions are unknown. The marked route has fixed anchors, recent reports, and a rescue station, although they have climbed it before. Which route should they take?
C: Theo could spend every Sunday this spring clearing irrigation channels by hand, improving water flow before the hot season and protecting his later harvest. The work is tedious and would replace his leisurely breakfasts and afternoons fishing at the lake. Should Theo maintain the channels each weekend?

A: Astronomer Peter needs to classify telescope images for ninety minutes each evening if he wants a complete dataset by spring. Tonight the work is monotonous, his apartment is warm, and a new detective series is ready to stream. Missing the session brings immediate relaxation but weakens the routine behind months of progress. Should Peter analyze the images or settle onto the sofa?
B: Swimmer Amina plans six months of early pool sessions to improve her turns before regional trials. Rain drums against the window at 5 a.m., and staying under the blankets would be far more pleasant than crossing town for repetitive drills, though another missed practice slows the improvement she wants. Should Amina get up and train or enjoy another two hours in bed?
C: A laboratory requires every researcher who misses equipment training to wait a month for the next session. Manager Colin learns that a new assistant was absent because she was caring for her injured father and will lose her summer placement if she waits, while others followed the rule. Should Colin arrange an exception for her or enforce the same schedule for everyone?

A: Illustrator Benicio wants his next exhibit to feature stark charcoal portraits, although his gallery owner and relatives prefer the bright landscapes that made him popular. They say the darker work will embarrass supporters attending the opening and may stop recommending him. Should Benicio show the portraits he wants to make or paint landscapes that preserve their approval?
B: Librarian Heather prefers to move the children's reading hour outdoors, where stories could include walks and noisy games. Her colleagues and parent committee expect the quiet indoor format and suggest she is being unprofessional by changing it. Should Heather run the lively outdoor program she favors or keep the familiar format to satisfy them?
C: Dancer Kwame receives an offer to join a celebrated contemporary company that could make him an international soloist. Its two-year tour would remove him from the small cultural center where he rehearses daily with childhood friends and teaches their children. Should Kwame accept the career-making tour or remain rooted in the artistic community that raised him?

A: A research institute removes anyone who misses two mandatory safety trainings from laboratory access. One technician missed the second session while caring for his wife during chemotherapy and asks to remain until the next course. Others lost access under the same rule. Should the director suspend him equally or grant an exception for his hardship?
B: A coding boot camp refunds tuition only when students withdraw during the first week. One participant asks for a late refund after becoming the sole carer for an injured parent, though earlier withdrawals received nothing. Returning her money would help with rent but break the known policy. Should the school enforce the deadline or show her mercy?
C: A planetary scientist is offered leadership of a celebrated observatory on another continent. The role would crown years of research and open major projects, but her partner cannot move and she would leave the close lab group that gathers at her home every week. Should she pursue the directorship or remain with the people who anchor her life?

A: A dairy farmer has stored enough feed to carry his herd through a forecast dry month. His neighbor's injured horse has gone without proper hay, and she cannot buy more until insurance pays. Sharing the feed would relieve the animal now but could leave his own cattle short. Should the farmer keep his full reserve or give her several bales?
B: Residents saved donations to repair the roof of their volunteer hall before autumn storms. A longtime volunteer needs a wheelchair ramp at home after an accident, and no public grant will arrive for months. Redirecting the fund would postpone the roof and risk water damage. Should the committee protect the hall budget or build the ramp for him now?
C: A young farmer can plant an unfamiliar heritage grain that may command a premium and reveal which crops suit the changing climate. Her insurer will cover only the standard wheat with predictable yields, which would protect the farm if summer turns harsh. Should she experiment with the untested grain or choose the insured crop and a safer harvest?

A: A social-app founder can earn a large acquisition bonus by enabling notifications designed to pull users back every few minutes. The feature will increase advertising revenue, but millions of users may lose attention and sleep as prompts interrupt work, study, and family time. Should she approve the notification system?
B: A fruit farmer can protect his profit during a pest outbreak by applying a cheap broad-spectrum pesticide. The treatment will also kill pollinating insects across surrounding fields and contaminate streams used by farms downstream, while a selective alternative costs much more. Which treatment should he use?
C: A freelance developer has saved enough to cover server fees through a slow business quarter. His former assistant needs immediate money for her son's hearing aid and has exhausted other options. Paying for it would help the child directly but could force the developer's service offline. Should he give her the savings?

A: Heavy rain is approaching, and orchard owner Tomas has one day to harvest pears for a supermarket order. Fast picking gets the fruit under cover but causes bruising and mixes unripe pears into crates; careful selection produces better boxes while leaving part of the crop exposed. Should Tomas harvest everything quickly or risk rain to maintain quality?
B: A museum asks programmer Nia to deliver its ticketing website before a holiday weekend. She can activate the tested booking pages now, or postpone launch to improve screen-reader navigation and verify complex group refunds, losing several busy days. Should Nia release the basic site on time or finish the slower, more dependable version?
C: Farmer Grace saved this season's reserve to repair a leaking barn roof before winter. Her hired shepherd's daughter needs an insulin pump that the family cannot afford, and paying for it would provide direct help but leave Grace's livestock and income exposed to storms. Should Grace fund the child's pump or preserve the farm's emergency reserve?

A: A dance company can improvise its outdoor finale among the audience, with performers choosing movements in response to the crowd. The approach might create an unforgettable performance, but a marked stage and fixed choreography would prevent collisions near the stone steps. Should the director embrace the open improvisation or use the controlled routine?
B: An engineer designing a weather app can let users combine experimental data feeds and build their own forecasts. That freedom may reveal useful patterns, although inconsistent sources could produce badly misleading results; a locked set of verified feeds would be dependable. Should she enable open-ended combinations or restrict forecasts to the protected configuration?
C: A photographer is invited to explain a portrait series by discussing the depression that shaped it. Sharing her diagnosis could deepen collaboration with the curator and help viewers understand the work, but it would expose medical information she has kept from colleagues. Should she disclose the personal history or let the photographs stand without revealing it?

A: Dr. Morgan can join a mobile clinic traveling between remote islands, where patient needs, housing, and weekly routes change constantly. Her hospital has offered a permanent outpatient post with regular hours, established equipment, and guaranteed renewal. Both begin next month; should she embrace the uncertain mobile practice or choose the protected hospital position?
B: Ibrahim has been invited to improvise live music for a traveling circus without seeing its program or knowing which cities will host it. His local orchestra instead offers a yearlong contract, rehearsed repertoire, and fixed pay. Should he accept the unpredictable collaboration or remain in the secure orchestral seat?
C: A physiotherapist promised to lead a mobility workshop for stroke survivors after two colleagues canceled. Hours before it begins, she develops a painful flare of rheumatoid arthritis that makes demonstrations difficult. Canceling leaves twelve patients without the instruction they arranged transport to attend. Should she protect her joints or deliver the workshop despite the flare?

A: Niko wants to build accessibility tools at a small software cooperative, where the work matches his interests and the pay is adequate. His former classmates expect him to join a famous technology firm and have already congratulated him on applying there. Choosing the cooperative could cost their admiration. Which offer should Niko accept?
B: After residency, Zoe wants to practice family medicine in a coastal village. Her supervising physicians and relatives push her toward cardiology at a prominent urban hospital, a choice they would respect and proudly announce. The village work feels more personally meaningful but less prestigious to them. Which career should Zoe pursue?
C: A coding bootcamp refunds tuition only to students who attend at least ninety percent of sessions, a published rule applied to everyone last term. Omar falls one class short because he accompanied his frightened mother to chemotherapy. Should the director grant his refund because of that hardship or enforce the attendance threshold equally?

A: During a winter night shift, a water technician develops sharp abdominal pain just as pressure drops across a housing estate. Leaving for urgent care protects him from a potentially serious condition, but residents may have no water until morning because he alone carries the access keys. Should he remain to locate the broken main?
B: A stage manager is still dizzy after striking her head during rehearsal, and her doctor advises two days without bright lights or noise. Tonight is the company's opening performance, with complicated cues that her inexperienced assistant has never called alone. Should she return backstage despite the symptoms?
C: Leah, a city librarian, wants to host a loud monthly zine workshop requested by local teenagers. Her colleagues prefer the quiet lecture series favored by trustees whose support influences her contract renewal. Running the workshop would fit Leah's own vision but risk their disapproval. Which program should she put on the calendar?

A: A laundry owner can increase his profit by replacing efficient machines with cheaper models that use twice as much water. The purchase lowers his immediate costs, but sustained consumption would strain the town's shared supply during recurring droughts. Should he choose the profitable machines or pay more to reduce the burden placed on other residents?
B: A race organizer can receive a sizeable personal commission by distributing single-use plastic bottles at every kilometer. Sponsors prefer the visibility, but tens of thousands of bottles would litter streets and require disposal after one morning. Should she accept the commission and bottle plan or forgo that income to reduce the event's collective waste?
C: A restaurant owner hopes to improve his pastry skills by completing a difficult recipe every night after closing. Ordering food and relaxing on the sofa would be easier and more enjoyable, while months of disciplined practice could expand next year's menu. Should he follow the nightly training plan or choose comfortable evenings without the extra effort?
