Should Aditi modernize specimen recording or continue the institute's traditional method?
B: At Raul's neighborhood shoe shop, customers have always watched repairs at a front workbench and talked with the cobbler. Moving production behind a wall would allow modern machinery and faster service, but longtime patrons treasure the visible craft as part of every visit. Should Raul redesign the shop around the new equipment or preserve its open workbench tradition?
C: A private company offers oceanographer Mae a generous fee to conduct coral surveys by helicopter, allowing her to finish quickly and accept more contracts. Boats would take longer and pay her less, but repeated flights consume far more fuel and add emissions whose effects fall broadly on coastal ecosystems and communities. Should Mae choose the lucrative helicopter surveys or use the slower, lower-impact boats?

A: Jonah can enter an accelerated doctoral program that promises early publications and a strong academic career, but its schedule would end the weekly study circle he has shared with three close classmates since freshman year. Staying in the regular program preserves those friendships and their mutual support but slows his progress. Should Jonah accelerate alone or continue alongside his study group?
B: The owner of a renowned vineyard has offered Amara an apprenticeship that could lead to managing her own estate. It begins during harvest, when her family's small farm relies on everyone working and eating together, a tradition that has kept the household close for decades. Should Amara take the vineyard opportunity or spend another harvest with her family?
C: A school board wants new history workbooks distributed before Monday so classes can start the revised curriculum on time. Editor Caleb found conflicting dates and poorly sourced maps that require another week to verify; delaying leaves teachers without materials, while printing now may put lasting errors in every classroom. Should Caleb approve immediate printing or hold the workbooks for careful correction?

A: A genetics team can publish a crop genome before a competing laboratory, giving breeders immediate access. Several sequences still have unresolved gaps, and another month of checking would produce a dependable reference while delaying its use and risking lost credit. Should the team publish now or finish validation?
B: A radiology department can issue screening results within twenty-four hours by having one physician read each scan. Waiting four days allows a second specialist to check subtle findings, but patients remain anxious and treatment referrals start later. Should the department favor rapid reports or double review?
C: A laboratory technician has an asthma flare on the night she promised to monitor a telescope during a rare lunar occultation. Rest and medication would protect her breathing, but leaving means collaborators lose observations they cannot repeat for decades. Should she remain at the telescope controls?

A: The maternity ward has recorded every newborn's footprint on a paper card kept by the family since the hospital opened. Director June proposes secure digital scans that are clearer and easier to retrieve, but nurses and parents value the inked card as a tangible rite. Should June replace the cards with digital records or preserve the footprint tradition?
B: A village orchestra has tuned to the same local pitch and opened concerts with its founder's march for generations. New conductor Pavel wants standard tuning and rotating contemporary openings so visiting musicians can join easily, while members fear losing their distinctive sound and ritual. Should Pavel modernize the orchestra's practice or continue its inherited musical customs?
C: A clinic removes patients from its waiting list after two missed appointments. Receptionist Alma learns that a homeless patient missed both because his shelter repeatedly changed locations; restoring him helps someone in hardship but bypasses others who complied and kept waiting. Should Alma make an exception for him or apply the same removal rule to every patient?

A: A neighborhood association gives Inez funds for a riverfront mural but no final design. She can invite residents to paint whatever develops over the weekend, risking a disjointed result, or hire a studio offering an approved sketch, insured painters, and guaranteed completion. Should Inez open the wall to uncertain collaboration or commission the predictable professional design?
B: Park ranger Cole can lead visitors into a newly opened wetland where wildlife sightings and trail conditions are unpredictable. The established boardwalk tour has railings, mapped stops, and a reliable return time but reveals little beyond familiar habitats. Should Cole offer the exploratory wetland walk or keep the group on the protected boardwalk route?
C: Organizer Fatima has been invited to direct a national housing coalition, a position that could give her campaigns far greater influence. Accepting requires leaving the tenant group whose members meet in her kitchen and have shared years of victories and setbacks. Should Fatima pursue the national leadership role or remain with her close neighborhood organization?

A: A ski resort offers racer Stefan free lodging and prize support if he promotes unrestricted helicopter skiing. The sponsorship would finance his season, while increased flights would burn fuel, disturb wildlife, and bring noise across valleys used by residents and other visitors. Should Stefan accept the valuable sponsorship or decline because of the wider impact?
B: Packaging supplier Rafi can double his margin by selling restaurants disposable foam containers that local rules still permit. The deal would stabilize his small company, but millions of boxes would enter landfills and litter waterways maintained by the wider community. Should Rafi take the profitable contract or keep selling costlier compostable packaging to limit collective harm?
C: Runner Elise prefers training for short trail races, although her parents and club mates insist she should enter a prestigious road marathon. They have already announced her expected participation and say withdrawing would disappoint everyone supporting her. Should Elise choose the smaller races she enjoys or run the marathon to preserve their approval?

A: A flood-relief charity needs a volunteer-matching app online by Friday. The developers can meet that date by releasing without testing on older phones, potentially excluding some users; another week would allow careful compatibility checks while volunteers continue using slow spreadsheets. Should the team launch quickly or delay until the app works reliably for everyone?
B: A school can distribute its new mathematics workbook before Monday’s term begins, but several examples have not been independently checked and diagrams remain unclear. A two-week delay allows teachers to correct and pilot every lesson, while pupils start without the promised materials. Should the principal issue it now or wait for a dependable edition?
C: A developer is offered leadership of a prestigious artificial-intelligence division in Singapore, a role that could define her career. Taking it means leaving the small company team and circle of cousins she sees several times a week for at least three years. Should she accept the advancement or preserve her close everyday relationships?

A: Fire inspector Calvin uses hearing aids but has hidden his hearing loss from coworkers. Explaining it could help the team communicate clearly during noisy inspections and make colleagues more candid about accommodations, yet the diagnosis is personal and may alter how they trust his judgment. Should Calvin disclose his hearing loss to the department or keep it confidential?
B: While leading a neighborhood flood committee, Soraya privately undergoes fertility treatment that often changes her availability. Telling volunteers could clarify sudden schedule changes and invite more honest planning, but it would expose a painful matter she has shared only with her partner. Should Soraya explain the treatment to the committee or keep her personal circumstances private?
C: Paramedic Lewis promised to cover a remote festival shift after two colleagues took leave. He wakes with severe vomiting, and withdrawing may leave the event below required medical staffing, but working twelve hours far from a hospital could dangerously worsen his dehydration. Should Lewis report for the duty he accepted or stay home to protect his health?

A: A school running track can reopen before next week's tournament if workers apply a thin surface that needs little curing time. Installing the full layered surface would postpone competition for a month but provide safer footing and withstand years of use. Which resurfacing plan should the school choose?
B: A peach grower can load fruit directly from the trees and reach the market before competitors, though bruised and underripe peaches may reach customers. Sorting each crate carefully would improve consistency but delay the shipment until prices fall. Should she ship immediately or complete the sorting?
C: To improve his balance before the next skating season, Anton must complete repetitive core exercises before breakfast five days a week. The routine promises gradual control, but it replaces the warm, unhurried mornings when he listens to music and stays in bed. Should Anton follow the training plan?

A: A theater replaces any actor who misses the final two rehearsals, and one understudy has already lost a role under that policy. Clara misses both because her apartment building burned down, yet asks to perform opening night. Should the director restore her role out of compassion or apply the same rule?
B: A field station assigns scarce telescope hours by a strict deadline, rejecting every late proposal this season. Dr. Okafor submits one day late after caring for a child hospitalized with meningitis, and the observations cannot wait another year. Should the committee accept his proposal exceptionally or uphold the deadline for all researchers?
C: A dancer promised to perform at a community fundraiser after ticket sales used her name. On the afternoon of the show, swelling in her ankle makes each landing painful, and continuing could extend the injury. Canceling may force refunds the organizers cannot cover. Should she protect her ankle or honor the performance commitment?

A: Darius wants to teach woodworking at a vocational college, where he enjoys helping apprentices master practical skills. His academic family expects him to accept a university history lectureship and regards vocational teaching as wasting his doctorate. Following his preference may bring years of disapproval at family gatherings. Which teaching post should Darius choose?
B: A neighborhood committee asks Lina to design either the modest reading garden she has carefully imagined or the large commemorative arch favored by influential residents. Building her garden may invite criticism and exclude her from future projects, while the arch would secure enthusiastic public approval. Which design should Lina recommend?
C: A teacher sees her closest colleague secretly give examination answers to a pupil whose scholarship depends on passing. When the headteacher asks whether anyone entered the classroom early, an accurate account could lead to her colleague’s dismissal. Claiming she saw nothing would protect a friend by concealing the misconduct. What should the teacher say?

A: A basketball league automatically suspends every player who receives three technical fouls. A teenager reaches the limit after shouting when he learned his brother had been hospitalized, and the suspension covers a final attended by scouts. Should officials apply the established penalty like they did for others or excuse him because of the crisis?
B: A field station charges all researchers who return equipment late because the next teams lose access. One graduate student was delayed rescuing an injured hiker and cannot afford the fee. Waiving it recognizes the emergency but treats her differently from previous late borrowers. Should the station collect the standard charge or make an exception?
C: A climbing coach can let trainees choose any route across a newly opened cliff, possibly discovering creative lines. A protected course with inspected anchors offers fewer surprises but sharply reduces uncertain falls and rescue delays. Should the coach permit free exploration of the cliff or require everyone to use the verified route?
